finding: There is no live range for this job on the site today (live is null), so this is a first build. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2017 Corolla about $246-$413; midsize 2017 Accord about $164-$302; truck 2021 F-150 about $164-$290; luxury 2015 Lexus ES 350 about $334-$518. A supportable range for mainstream vehicles is therefore about $165-$415, and about $335-$520 for a luxury sedan like the example. The two general benchmarks sit inside or just above that: FIXD $297-$352 is inside it, and YourMechanic's Blazer examples ($308-$425 mobile, up to $693 at a shop) reach above it. RepairPal's BMW X6 figure ($899-$1,118) is far above our luxury total, which shows that large European luxury vehicles, where the motor comes with its linkage or sits deep under the cowl, can cost about double the example here; no parts were loaded for one, so the luxury range should be read as a Japanese luxury sedan only. Parts: every high is a genuine list price from a dealer catalog page for the example vehicle and year ($252.81 Corolla, $142.38 Accord, $130.18 F-150, $357.60 ES 350). Every low is the lowest verified discounted price of the same genuine motor, not an aftermarket price, because no new aftermarket motor naming an example vehicle and year was found on a page that would load; the only new aftermarket motors seen ($128-$132) printed no fitment. Aftermarket motors probably exist for these cars and could bring the low ends down. The luxury class still has a single parts source; a second search found only the same seller and used parts. How solid the labor times are, stated plainly. Every low end is now a manufacturer's warranty time printed with the unit for removing and replacing the windshield wiper motor, but only the truck's is for the example vehicle: Ford allows 0.7 Hours on the 2021-2022 F-150. The other three lows are for comparable vehicles, not the examples, which is why confidence stays low: Mitsubishi allows 0.6 hours on the 2011-2015 Outlander Sport (used for the economy class) and 0.6 hours on the 2007-2013 Outlander (midsize), each for the motor alone, and FCA allows 0.6 hours on the 2018 Alfa Romeo Stelvio (luxury), where the motor is replaced as one unit with its linkage. Four maker times of 0.6-0.7 hours on four different vehicles agree closely; no Toyota, Honda or Lexus time with a unit was found. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill. Every high end is one general figure: a wiper motor tip sheet on a parts maker's site prints a replacement time of under 1 hour for a service technician, so 1 hour is used as the ceiling; it is not a flat-rate book time and not for any example vehicle. An online parts seller's unsigned do-it-yourself guide says 1 to 1.5 hours, and FIXD says 30 to 90 minutes (another estimator, so not used); a shop that bills 1.5 hours would add about $60-$80 to the high ends above. Older maker figures printed without a unit point the same way (Honda 0.7 to inspect and fit a wiper motor kit on a 2003 Accord, GM 0.5 to fit a wiper module with inspection on a 2014-2015 Equinox). This is an estimate, never a quote and never a diagnosis.
extras: A quote often adds diagnosis (a dead wiper can be a fuse, relay, switch, control module or seized linkage, not the motor), shop supplies and sales tax. The wiper linkage (transmission) is often worn or seized when the motor fails and may be quoted with it; on some vehicles the motor is sold only with the linkage, which raises the part price (on the 2021 F-150 the assembly with linkage lists at $434.55 against $130.18 for the motor alone). New wiper blades or arms, a cowl panel clip or seal broken on removal, and the rear wiper motor are separate.
